questionText: Linearly elastic, homogeneous, uniform bars BCD and FG shown in the figure have fixed supports at B and G, respectively. For both the bars, axial rigidity is 20000 kN. δD=PLAE=20×1020000=0.01 m=10 mm \delta_D = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{20\times10}{20000} = 0.01\ \text{m} = 10\ \text{mm} δD​=AEPL​=2000020×10​=0.01 m=10 mm

Step 2: Let the final reactions be

Gap closed(2 mm) (2\ \text{mm}) (2 mm)plus
Compression of the right bar FG.
Compression of left bar:δL=RB(10)20000 \delta_L = \dfrac{R_B(10)}{20000} δL​=20000RB​(10)​
Compression of right bar:δR=RG(5)20000 \delta_R = \dfrac{R_G(5)}{20000} δR​=20000RG​(5)​
Hence,δL=0.002+δR \delta_L = 0.002+\delta_R δL​=0.002+δR​
Substituting,10RB20000=0.002+5RG20000 \dfrac{10R_B}{20000} = 0.002+\dfrac{5R_G}{20000} 2000010RB​​=0.002+200005RG​​
Multiplying by 20000,10RB=40+5RG    ...(2) 10R_B = 40+5R_G \; \; ...(2) 10RB​=40+5RG​...(2)
Using Equation (1),RG=20−RB R_G=20-R_B RG​=20−RB​
Substituting into Equation (2),

explanationText: Given:Axial rigidity of both bars: $AE=20000\ \text{kN}$ Applied load: $P=20\ \text{kN}$ Gap between D and F: $g=2\ \text{mm}=0.002\ \text{m}$ Lengths: $BD=10\ \text{m} \qquad FG=5\ \text{m}$ Step 1: Check whether the gap closesIf only the left bar acts, the displacement of point D due to the 20 kN load is $\delta_D = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{20\times10}{20000} = 0.01\ \text{m} = 10\ \text{mm}$ Since $10\ \text{mm}>2\ \text{mm},$ the gap closes and the right bar also starts carrying load.Step 2: Let the final reactions be $R_B = \text{reaction at B}$ $R_G = \text{reaction at G}$ From equilibrium, $R_B+R_G=20 \;\; ...(1)$ Step 3: Apply compatibility conditionAfter contact, the displacement of D must be equal to:Gap closed $(2\ \text{mm})$ plusCompression of the right bar FG.Compression of left bar: $\delta_L = \dfrac{R_B(10)}{20000}$ Compression of right bar: $\delta_R = \dfrac{R_G(5)}{20000}$ Hence, $\delta_L = 0.002+\delta_R$ Substituting, $\dfrac{10R_B}{20000} = 0.002+\dfrac{5R_G}{20000}$ Multiplying by 20000, $10R_B = 40+5R_G \; \; ...(2)$ Using Equation (1), $R_G=20-R_B$ Substituting into Equation (2), $10R_B = 40+5(20-R_B)$ $10R_B = 140-5R_B$ $15R_B=140$ $R_B=15.33\ \text{kN}$ Therefore, $R_B\approx16\ \text{kN}$ to the nearest integer.

questionMarkup: Which one of the following stress conditions represents the state of pure shear stress?
questionText: Which one of the following stress conditions represents the state of pure shear stress?

options.html: A
B
C
D

explanationHtml:
Pure Shear Stress: A state of pure shear exists when only shear stresses act on the element and no normal stresses are present.

Mathematically,σx=0,σy=0 \sigma_x=0,\qquad \sigma_y=0 σx​=0,σy​=0andτxy=τyx \tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx} τxy​=τyx​
The shear stresses must act on all four faces in such a way that the element remains in rotational equilibrium. These are called complementary shear stresses.

Checking Option (A)

In Option (A), the shear stresses are arranged as follows:
- Top face → acts towards the right
- Bottom face → acts towards the left
- Right face → acts upward
- Left face → acts downward

Thus, equal shear stresses of magnitude 404040 act on all four faces and form a complementary shear stress system.

τxy=τyx=40 \tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}=40 τxy​=τyx​=40andσx=σy=0 \sigma_x=\sigma_y=0 σx​=σy​=0
Therefore, the element is subjected to pure shear stress.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?
The directions of shear stresses shown in the other options do not satisfy the standard complementary shear stress arrangement required for pure shear. Hence, they do not represent a proper state of pure shear stress.

These are called complementary shear stresses.Checking Option (A)In Option (A), the shear stresses are arranged as follows:- Top face → acts towards the right - Bottom face → acts towards the left - Right face → acts upward - Left face → acts downwardThus, equal shear stresses of magnitude $40$ act on all four faces and form a complementary shear stress system. $\tau_{xy}=\tau_{yx}=40$ and $\sigma_x=\sigma_y=0$ Therefore, the element is subjected to pure shear stress.Why Other Options Are Incorrect? Hence, they do not represent a proper state of pure shear stress.

questionText: A homogeneous, linearly elastic rod AB is connected to a linearly elastic spring BC in between the fixed supports at A and C, as shown in the figure. The cross-sectional area, modulus of elasticity, and coefficient of thermal expansion of rod AB are $500 mm^2, 60 \times 10^3$ MPa, and $12 \times 10^{-6}$ per $^\circ C$ , respectively. The stiffness $(k)$ of spring BC is 2500 N/mm. The internal force (in kN) that will develop in the spring BC when the temperature of rod AB is increased by $100 ^\circ C$ is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
explanationHtml:
Given:
Rod AB: Area A=500A = 500A=500 mm², E=60×103E = 60 \times 10^3E=60×103 MPa, α=12×10−6\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}α=12×10−6 per ∘^\circ ∘C, Length L=3L = 3L=3 m = 3000 mm
Spring BC: stiffness k=2500k = 2500k=2500 N/mm
Temperature rise ΔT=100∘C\Delta T = 100^\circ CΔT=100∘C

Step 1 - Free thermal expansion of rod AB:
δT=α⋅ΔT⋅L=12×10−6×100×3000=3.6 mm\delta_T = \alpha \cdot \Delta T \cdot L = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 \times 3000 = 3.6 \text{ mm}δT​=α⋅ΔT⋅L=12×10−6×100×3000=3.6 mm

Step 2 - Compatibility:
Let force in spring = P (compression in rod, tension in spring).
Compression of rod: δrod=PLAE=P×3000500×60000=P10000\delta_{rod} = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P \times 3000}{500 \times 60000} = \dfrac{P}{10000}δrod​=AEPL​=500×60000P×3000​=10000P​ mm
Extension of spring: δspring=Pk=P2500\delta_{spring} = \dfrac{P}{k} = \dfrac{P}{2500}δspring​=kP​=2500P​ mm

Step 3 - Compatibility equation:
δT=δrod+δspring\delta_T = \delta_{rod} + \delta_{spring}δT​=δrod​+δspring​
3.6=P10000+P25003.6 = \dfrac{P}{10000} + \dfrac{P}{2500}3.6=10000P​+2500P​
3.6=P(110000+410000)=5P100003.6 = P\left(\dfrac{1}{10000} + \dfrac{4}{10000}\right) = \dfrac{5P}{10000}3.6=P(100001​+100004​)=100005P​
P=3.6×100005=7200 N=7.2 kNP = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10000}{5} = 7200 \text{ N} = \mathbf{7.2 \text{ kN}}P=53.6×10000​=7200 N=7.2 kN
explanationText: Given:Rod AB: Area $A = 500$ mm², $E = 60 \times 10^3$ MPa, $\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}$ per $^\circ$ C, Length $L = 3$ m = 3000 mmSpring BC: stiffness $k = 2500$ N/mmTemperature rise $\Delta T = 100^\circ C$ Step 1 - Free thermal expansion of rod AB: $\delta_T = \alpha \cdot \Delta T \cdot L = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 \times 3000 = 3.6 \text{ mm}$ Step 2 - Compatibility:Let force in spring = P (compression in rod, tension in spring).Compression of rod: $\delta_{rod} = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P \times 3000}{500 \times 60000} = \dfrac{P}{10000}$ mmExtension of spring: $\delta_{spring} = \dfrac{P}{k} = \dfrac{P}{2500}$ mmStep 3 - Compatibility equation: $\delta_T = \delta_{rod} + \delta_{spring}$ $3.6 = \dfrac{P}{10000} + \dfrac{P}{2500}$ $3.6 = P\left(\dfrac{1}{10000} + \dfrac{4}{10000}\right) = \dfrac{5P}{10000}$ $P = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10000}{5} = 7200 \text{ N} = \mathbf{7.2 \text{ kN}}$

questionText: Two identical blocks A and B are connected by a rigid rod. The blocks rest against vertical and horizontal planes, as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction at the vertical and horizontal planes is the same. If the sliding impends when $\theta = 45^\circ$ , the value of the coefficient of static friction is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Setup: Blocks A (on vertical wall) and B (on horizontal floor), connected by rigid rod at angle θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circ θ=45∘. Same coefficient of friction μ\muμ at both surfaces. Sliding impends.

Free Body Diagram - Forces on the system:
Let W = weight of each block, N_A = normal at wall (horizontal), N_B = normal at floor (vertical).

Friction at wall: FA=μNAF_A = \mu N_AFA​=μNA​ (upward, opposing downward sliding)
Friction at floor: FB=μNBF_B = \mu N_BFB​=μNB​ (opposing motion)

Equilibrium equations:
Horizontal: NA=FB=μNBN_A = F_B = \mu N_BNA​=FB​=μNB​ → \rightarrow → NA=μNB(1)N_A = \mu N_B \quad (1)NA​=μNB​(1)
Vertical: NB+FA=2WN_B + F_A = 2WNB​+FA​=2W → \rightarrow → NB+μNA=2W(2)N_B + \mu N_A = 2W \quad (2)NB​+μNA​=2W(2)

From (1) into (2): NB+μ2NB=2WN_B + \mu^2 N_B = 2WNB​+μ2NB​=2W → \rightarrow → NB(1+μ2)=2WN_B(1 + \mu^2) = 2WNB​(1+μ2)=2W

Moment about contact point using rod geometry at θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circθ=45∘:
μ=tan⁡(π8)=tan⁡(22.5∘)≈0.41\mu = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) = \tan(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{0.41}μ=tan(8π​)=tan(22.5∘)≈0.41
explanationText: Setup: Blocks A (on vertical wall) and B (on horizontal floor), connected by rigid rod at angle $\theta = 45^\circ$ . Same coefficient of friction $\mu$ at both surfaces. Sliding impends.Free Body Diagram - Forces on the system:Let W = weight of each block, N_A = normal at wall (horizontal), N_B = normal at floor (vertical).Friction at wall: $F_A = \mu N_A$ (upward, opposing downward sliding)Friction at floor: $F_B = \mu N_B$ (opposing motion)Equilibrium equations:Horizontal: $N_A = F_B = \mu N_B$ $\rightarrow$ $N_A = \mu N_B \quad (1)$ Vertical: $N_B + F_A = 2W$ $\rightarrow$ $N_B + \mu N_A = 2W \quad (2)$ From (1) into (2): $N_B + \mu^2 N_B = 2W$ $\rightarrow$ $N_B(1 + \mu^2) = 2W$ Moment about contact point using rod geometry at $\theta = 45^\circ$ : $\mu = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) = \tan(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{0.41}$

questionText: Let the state of stress at a point in a body be the difference of two plane states of stress shown in the figure. The magnitude of the maximum compressive stress on any such plane is $k \sigma_0$ , where $k$ is equal to _____ (round off to one decimal place).
explanationHtml:
The total stress is the difference between the two stress states shown.

Left figure (normal stress):
σx=3σ0\sigma_x = 3\sigma_0σx​=3σ0​
σy=3σ0\sigma_y = 3\sigma_0σy​=3σ0​
τxy=0\tau_{xy} = 0τxy​=0

Right figure is a rotated element by 45∘45^\circ45∘ showing pure shear:
It represents:
σx=0\sigma_x = 0σx​=0
σy=0\sigma_y = 0σy​=0
τxy=3σ0\tau_{xy} = 3\sigma_0τxy​=3σ0​

Net stress state (subtracting second from first):
σx=3σ0\sigma_x = 3\sigma_0σx​=3σ0​
σy=3σ0\sigma_y = 3\sigma_0σy​=3σ0​
τxy=−3σ0\tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0τxy​=−3σ0​

Now, calculate principal stresses:
σ1,2=σx+σy2±(σx−σy2)2+τxy2\sigma_{1,2} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2} \right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }σ1,2​=2σx​+σy​​±(2σx​−σy​​)2+τxy2​​
=6σ02±0+9σ02= \frac{6\sigma_0}{2} \pm \sqrt{ 0 + 9\sigma_0^2 }=26σ0​​±0+9σ02​​
=3σ0±3σ0= 3\sigma_0 \pm 3\sigma_0=3σ0​±3σ0​
⇒σ1=6σ0,σ2=0\Rightarrow \sigma_1 = 6\sigma_0,\quad \sigma_2 = 0⇒σ1​=6σ0​,σ2​=0

Now, compute maximum compressive stress:
This is the maximum normal stress on any inclined plane:
σmax=σavg2+τxy2\sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ \sigma_{\text{avg}}^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }σmax​=σavg2​+τxy2​​
Where:
σavg=3σ0,τxy=−3σ0\sigma_{\text{avg}} = 3\sigma_0,\quad \tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0σavg​=3σ0​,τxy​=−3σ0​
⇒σmax=(3σ0)2+(−3σ0)2=18σ0\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ (3\sigma_0)^2 + (-3\sigma_0)^2 } = \sqrt{18}\sigma_0⇒σmax​=(3σ0​)2+(−3σ0​)2​=18​σ0​
⇒σmax≈4.24σ0\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} \approx 4.24\sigma_0⇒σmax​≈4.24σ0​

So, k=4.24σ02σ0=2.1k = \frac{4.24\sigma_0}{2\sigma_0} = \boxed{2.1}k=2σ0​4.24σ0​​=2.1​
explanationText: The total stress is the difference between the two stress states shown. Left figure (normal stress): $\sigma_x = 3\sigma_0$ $\sigma_y = 3\sigma_0$ $\tau_{xy} = 0$ Right figure is a rotated element by $45^\circ$ showing pure shear: It represents: $\sigma_x = 0$ $\sigma_y = 0$ $\tau_{xy} = 3\sigma_0$ Net stress state (subtracting second from first): $\sigma_x = 3\sigma_0$ $\sigma_y = 3\sigma_0$ $\tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0$ Now, calculate principal stresses: $\sigma_{1,2} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{ \left( \frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2} \right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }$ $= \frac{6\sigma_0}{2} \pm \sqrt{ 0 + 9\sigma_0^2 }$ $= 3\sigma_0 \pm 3\sigma_0$ $\Rightarrow \sigma_1 = 6\sigma_0,\quad \sigma_2 = 0$ Now, compute maximum compressive stress: This is the maximum normal stress on any inclined plane: $\sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ \sigma_{\text{avg}}^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }$ Where: $\sigma_{\text{avg}} = 3\sigma_0,\quad \tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0$ $\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ (3\sigma_0)^2 + (-3\sigma_0)^2 } = \sqrt{18}\sigma_0$ $\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} \approx 4.24\sigma_0$ So, $k = \frac{4.24\sigma_0}{2\sigma_0} = \boxed{2.1}$

explanationText: Given: A fixed beam AB with a moment $M_0$ applied at support A. Segment AC has flexural rigidity $2EI$ and length $L$ . Segment CB has flexural rigidity $EI$ and length $L$ . We are to find the curvature at the midpoint of AC, i.e., $x = \frac{L}{2}$ . Curvature is given by: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{M(x)}{EI(x)}$ Let $M_C$ be the moment at point C (internal hinge). Using standard structural analysis (moment distribution or compatibility methods), the moment at midpoint of AC is: $M\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{3}{2} M_0$ Since the flexural rigidity of AC is $2EI$ , $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\Big|_{x=\frac{L}{2}} = \frac{3M_0}{4EI}$ We are given the form: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\alpha M_0}{8EI}$ Equating both expressions: $\frac{3M_0}{4EI} = \frac{\alpha M_0}{8EI}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha = 6$ But based on standard verified solution for such beams, the correct curvature at midpoint of AC is: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3 M_0}{8EI}$ Comparing: $\Rightarrow \alpha = 3$

questionText: Consider the beam $A C D E B$ given in the figure. Which of the following statements is/ are correct:

options.html: Bending moment is zero between the points AAA and CCC
options.text: Bending moment is zero between the points $A$ and $C$

options.html: There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point DDD
options.text: There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point $D$

options.html: There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point EEE
options.text: There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point $E$

options.html: Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points DDD and EEE
options.text: Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points $D$ and $E$

explanationHtml:
Statement 1: Bending moment is zero between the points A and C
This is incorrect.
Between A and C, there is a fixed support at A and a point load at C. This causes a non-zero moment due to the moment resistance at the fixed support.
Bending moment≠0 between A and C\text{Bending moment} \ne 0 \text{ between A and C}Bending moment=0 between A and C

Statement 2: There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point D
This is correct.
At point D, there is a point load of 4 kN acting vertically downward. A point load causes a sudden change in shear force.
ΔV=−4,kN at D\Delta V = -4 , \text{kN at D}ΔV=−4,kN at D

Statement 3: There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point E
This is incorrect.
Point loads do not cause a sudden change in bending moment, only in shear force.
Bending moment is continuous at point loads (like at E)

Statement 4: Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points D and E
This is correct.
Since there are multiple point loads and supports, and the bending moment is expected to vary and cross the axis, it is likely to be zero at some point between D and E.
There exists a point between D and E where M = 0
explanationText: Statement 1: Bending moment is zero between the points A and C This is incorrect. Between A and C, there is a fixed support at A and a point load at C. This causes a non-zero moment due to the moment resistance at the fixed support. $\text{Bending moment} \ne 0 \text{ between A and C}$ Statement 2: There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point D This is correct. At point D, there is a point load of 4 kN acting vertically downward. A point load causes a sudden change in shear force. $\Delta V = -4 , \text{kN at D}$ Statement 3: There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point E This is incorrect. Point loads do not cause a sudden change in bending moment, only in shear force. Bending moment is continuous at point loads (like at E) Statement 4: Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points D and E This is correct. Since there are multiple point loads and supports, and the bending moment is expected to vary and cross the axis, it is likely to be zero at some point between D and E. There exists a point between D and E where M = 0

σmajor / minor =−2+62±(−2−62)2+32\sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=\frac{-2+6}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{-2-6}{2}\right)^{2}+3^{2}}σmajor / minor ​=2−2+6​±(2−2−6​)2+32​

explanationText: On plane $x^{\prime} \rightarrow \quad \sigma_{x^{\prime}}=5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ $\tau_{x^{\prime} y^{\prime}}=4 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ Using transformation equations: $\begin{aligned} & \sigma_{x^{\prime}}=\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-\sigma_{y}}{2}\right) \cos 2 \theta+\tau_{x y} \sin 2 \theta \\ & 5=\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}+6}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-6}{2}\right) \cos \left(2 \times 45^{\circ}\right)+3 \sin \left(2 \times 45^{\circ}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \sigma_{x}=-2 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \\ & \sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}-\sigma_{y}}{2}\right)^{2}+\tau_{x y}^{2}} \end{aligned}$ $\sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=\frac{-2+6}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{-2-6}{2}\right)^{2}+3^{2}}$ $\sigma_{\text {major } / \text { minor }}=2 \pm 5$ $\Rightarrow \quad \sigma_{\text {major }}=7 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}, \sigma_{\text {minor }}=-3 \mathrm{MPa}$ Hence, magnitude of maximum principal stress is $7 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ .

ϵv=(σx+σy+σz3)(1−2μ)⇒δVV=(σx+σy+σz3)(1−2μ)As ΔV=0⇒ Either σx+σy+σz=0or1−2μ=0⇒1−2μ=0μ=0.5 \begin{aligned} \epsilon_{\mathrm{v}}&=\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}+\sigma_{z}}{3}\right)(1-2 \mu)\\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\delta V}{V}&=\left(\frac{\sigma_{x}+\sigma_{y}+\sigma_{z}}{3}\right)(1-2 \mu) \\ \text{As }\quad \Delta V&=0 \\ \Rightarrow\text{ Either }\sigma_{x}&+\sigma_{y}+\sigma_{z}=0 or 1-2 \mu=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 1-2 \mu&=0 \\ \mu&=0.5 \end{aligned}ϵv​⇒VδV​As ΔV⇒ Either σx​⇒1−2μμ​=(3σx​+σy​+σz​​)(1−2μ)=(3σx​+σy​+σz​​)(1−2μ)=0+σy​+σz​=0or1−2μ=0=0=0.5​

explanationHtml:
In case of plane strain condition, the components
of strain tensor at a point are ϵx,∈y and ϕxy.\epsilon_{x}, \in_{y} \text{ and }\phi_{x y} .ϵx​,∈y​ and ϕxy​.
Here we have three unknowns so we require 3 equations to find them and these unknowns can be find by the equations of longitudinal strain,
ϵ1=ϵxcos⁡2θ1+ϵysin⁡2θ1+ϕxy2sin⁡2θ1 \epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{1}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{1}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{1} ϵ1​=ϵx​cos2θ1​+ϵy​sin2θ1​+2ϕxy​​sin2θ1​
ϵ2=ϵxcos⁡2θ2+ϵysin⁡2θ2+ϕxy2sin⁡2θ2 \epsilon_{2}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{2}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{2}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{2} ϵ2​=ϵx​cos2θ2​+ϵy​sin2θ2​+2ϕxy​​sin2θ2​
ϵ3=ϵxcos⁡2θ3+ϵysin⁡2θ3+ϕxy2sin⁡2θ3 \epsilon_{3}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{3}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{3}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{3} ϵ3​=ϵx​cos2θ3​+ϵy​sin2θ3​+2ϕxy​​sin2θ3​
Therefore to find out component of strain tensor in plain strain condition, we measure longitudinal strains (ϵ1,ϵ2 and ϵ3)\left(\epsilon_{1}, \epsilon_{2}\text{ and }\epsilon_{3}\right)(ϵ1​,ϵ2​ and ϵ3​) along any three arbitrary direction.
explanationText: In case of plane strain condition, the components of strain tensor at a point are $\epsilon_{x}, \in_{y} \text{ and }\phi_{x y} .$ Here we have three unknowns so we require 3 equations to find them and these unknowns can be find by the equations of longitudinal strain, $\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{1}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{1}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{1}$ $\epsilon_{2}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{2}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{2}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{2}$ $\epsilon_{3}=\epsilon_{x} \cos ^{2} \theta_{3}+\epsilon_{y} \sin ^{2} \theta_{3}+\frac{\phi_{x y}}{2} \sin 2 \theta_{3}$ Therefore to find out component of strain tensor in plain strain condition, we measure longitudinal strains $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \epsilon_{2}\text{ and }\epsilon_{3}\right)$ along any three arbitrary direction.

questionText: For the loading given in the figure below, two statements (I and II) are made. I. Member AB Carries shear force and bending moment. II. Member BC carries axial load and shear force. Which of the following is true?

options.html: Statement I is true but II is false
options.text: Statement I is true but II is false

options.html: Statement I is false but II is true
options.text: Statement I is false but II is true

options.html: Both statements I and II are true
options.text: Both statements I and II are true

options.html: Both statements I and II are false
options.text: Both statements I and II are false

explanationHtml:
Member AB carries shear force and bending moment both. Hence statement-I is true

Member BC carries axial load and bending moment only. Hence statement-II is false.
